answer:
FINAL ANSWER (natural-language hypothesis):

The variable is the respondent's RACE — specifically the White-vs-non-White (majority) contrast, i.e., SAMPLE_RACE. In this NLS sample, the effect of being White on BA degree completion is large and highly significant in isolation; once SES and academic characteristics (the ASVAB-composite ability score and class percentile) are added to the analysis, that effect collapses by more than a factor of five (≈13× in this file) and becomes statistically insignificant — i.e., the racial gap in BA completion is essentially explained by socioeconomic status and academic preparation rather than by race itself.

Concretely (logistic coefficients, the only scale on which 0.50-level effects can arise given 2.7% BA prevalence):
• Bivariate model (BA ~ White): coefficient = +0.9735, p < 0.0001.
• Full model (BA ~ White + SES + ASVAB composite + class percentile): coefficient = +0.0741 (≈ 0.09), p = 0.68 — no longer significant; >5× (13.1×) drop.
• The collapse specifically requires BOTH academic characteristics: with class rank alone the White coefficient stays +0.57 (p = 0.001); with both ASVAB score and class rank it falls to ~0.07–0.00 (ns).

Caveat stated plainly: no candidate in this provided CSV reproduces both target figures exactly. The full-model target (≈0.0923 ns) is matched closely by RACE (+0.0741, p=0.68), but the bivariate White coefficient here is 0.97 rather than 0.5024 (it is ≈0.48–0.57 under alternative standard race codings). Under the agreed tie-break — the wording "when both SES and academic characteristics are included" frames SES and academics as the added controls, so the focal must be a distinct social-background factor whose association collapses — RACE is the only qualifying candidate: FAMILY SIZE matches the 0.5024 magnitude (−0.5077) but does NOT decrease (stays −0.51, significant), and SEX never reaches ~0.50 (bivariate 0.20, p=0.13). SES is the best numeric runner-up (biv +0.47) but is excluded by the tie-break and fails the canonical model (it flips to −0.22, p=0.03, significant when both ASVAB and class rank are controlled).

payload.hypothesis: The variable is the respondent's race (SAMPLE_RACE) — the White-vs-non-White contrast. The log-odds effect of being White on BA degree completion is large and significant on its own (+0.9735, p<0.0001) but collapses ~13x to +0.0741 (p=0.68, not significant, ~ the target 0.0923) once SES and academic characteristics (ASVAB composite score and class percentile) are controlled — i.e., the racial gap in BA completion is largely explained by socioeconomic status and academic preparation.
payload.workflow: 1) Inspection: N=8773, 9 columns, zero missingness; BA rate 2.7%; all point-biserial correlations with BA <=0.18 so effects read as logistic coefficients. 2) Two-model design: A = bivariate logit of BA on each focal; B = BA ~ focal + SES + ASVAB + PERCENTILE (canonical), with sensitivity variants (academics={PCT},{ASVAB},{both}; +social background; logit/probit/OLS). 3) Enumerated focals: RACE(White/Black/Hispanic/Minority), SEX, FAMILY SIZE, SES, ASVAB, PERCENTILE. 4) Scored each on proximity to bivariate 0.5024, full-model ~0.00-0.15 with p>0.05, positive sign, consistency with 'SES-as-control' wording. 5) Result: RACE (White vs non-White) is the only social-background focal (SES as control) that collapses to ~0.07-0.00 (ns) — only when BOTH academic characteristics enter; FAMILY SIZE disqualified (no decline), SES runner-up (numeric fit but excluded by wording and sign-flip under canonical model). 6) Score table and script saved as artifacts.
